headline: Thousands Remain Without Power After Thanksgiving Day Storm

paragraphs.text: At a fire station in White Lake, N.Y., Chief Charlie Stackhouse handed out bags of dry ice and water to residents who remained without power on Saturday after a powerful storm on Thanksgiving battered states from Virginia to New Jersey.
Along the East Coast, about 88,000 customers remained without power on Saturday, according to PowerOutage.us. At one point on Thursday, more than 750,000 customers were without power in the region.
Volunteer firefighters in White Lake — a hamlet in the Town of Bethel in the Catskills — responded to downed trees and power lines after high winds and rain ripped through the area.
By Saturday, the storm was over, but some residents were still trying to keep food from spoiling. New York State Electric and Gas provided dry ice and water.
“Today’s more recovery efforts,” Chief Stackhouse said. “Some of our people that haven’t had power have been told that their restoration time is either sometime tomorrow or sometime Monday.”
Not everyone who regained electricity was able to keep it, he said. Utility workers have had to turn off power to safely restore it to other areas in a controlled fashion.
“Unfortunately, we are kind of used to this around here,” Chief Stackhouse said.
The area is dense with trees that can fall and rip down power lines during high winds. This most recent bout of severe weather was particularly widespread.
“We haven’t had dry ice that we’ve had to hand out for the last several storms there’s been outages,” he said. “This one’s a little bit longer to restore.”
The Weather Prediction Center said on Saturday that the Thanksgiving storm system was weakening and moving away from New England and the central Appalachians.
By Friday night, about 205,000 customers remained without electricity from North Carolina to New Hampshire, with a majority in Pennsylvania.

Even as the numbers of outages ticked down, rural communities still posted notices on social media of warming shelters and charging stations. The government of Sullivan County, which includes White Lake, on Saturday notified residents of where they could escape the cold.

In Arrowhead Lake, Pa., which has a population of about 1,000 people and is roughly 24 miles south of Scranton, more than 800 customers in the area were without power as of early Saturday afternoon, according to PPL Electric Utilities, which serves the area.

In nearby Pocono Lake, some homes were still without electricity even as most had it restored, said Keli Youngblood, an associate at the Locust Lake Village property owner’s association, which has about 1,200 homes.
“We have our common chalet that has a generator open for people that need it,” Ms. Youngblood said on Saturday.
She said her home’s power went out on Thanksgiving for about 12 hours, and she and her family bundled under blankets.
Utility companies across the affected states said their crews would work through the weekend to restore power as long as conditions were safe.
“We were very lucky,” Ms. Youngblood added. “But I know that there’s a lot of people in the area who it did definitely disrupt their plans. They were halfway through cooking a turkey.”

The storm brought heavy rain — one to four inches in some areas — on Thursday afternoon in Delaware, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Virginia before it moved to New Jersey and New York in the evening. Some parts of the Carolinas recorded more than nine inches of rain.
On Saturday afternoon, about 30,000 customers were still without power in Missouri, according to PowerOutage.us, after forecasters said as much as 15 inches of snow fell on Thursday.
Even though the storm had passed, Chief Stackhouse said dangers remained as trees were down and low-hanging wires remain energized.
“A lot of people do have generators and they’re just kind of doing what they can,” he said.
